# Ostwald Used the Principle Without the Name

To take in the importance of Peirce's principle, one must get accustomed to applying it to concrete cases.[^1] Ostwald, the illustrious Leipzig chemist, had been making perfectly distinct use of the principle of pragmatism in his lectures on the philosophy of science, tho he had not called it by that name.[^2]

"All realities influence our practice," he wrote,[^3] "and that influence is their meaning for us.[^4] I am accustomed to put questions to my classes in this way: In what respects would the world be different if this alternative or that were true?[^5] If I can find nothing that would become different, then the alternative has no sense."[^6]

That is, the rival views mean practically the same thing, and meaning, other than practical, there is for us none.[^7]
